summary: Revelio is a two-stage harness for C/C++ memory-safety bug hunting. A cheap model (Haiku 4.5), helped by lightweight static preprocessing, generates and ranks per-file vulnerability hypotheses. A stronger model (Sonnet 4.6) then has to build an executable Proof-of-Vulnerability that a sanitizer confirms before anything is reported. The paper reports 19 zero-days in 7 long-fuzzed OSS-Fuzz projects for about $300, and 175 validated vulnerabilities on 100 CyberGym projects versus 31–55 for Claude Code, Codex and Sorcar at similar cost.

claims.claim: Revelio finds 19 previously unknown memory-safety vulnerabilities (7 CVEs) in 7 OSS-Fuzz projects for ~$300 total, ~1 hour per project.
claims.evidence: Table III and §V-A; $42/project median and ~$16 per manually validated vulnerability (§V-A text). Projects are 'randomly selected' but only 7; disclosure-backed CVEs provide external validation.

claims.claim: On 100 CyberGym projects Revelio finds 175 validated vulnerabilities vs 55 (Claude Code), 39 (Codex), 31 (Sorcar), with 69% recall of known bugs and 0% FP at similar cost.
claims.evidence: Table VIII: Revelio 175 found, $9.10/vuln, 69% recall, 0% FP; Claude Code 55, $16.20, 53%, 49% FP; Codex 39, $8.96, 39%, 60% FP; Sorcar 31, $6.27, 31%, 28% FP. File-localized protocol reveals the vulnerable file (easier than CyberGym Level 0). Baselines receive a natural-language pipeline prompt (T2) rather than an enforced sanitizer loop; part of Claude Code results used Opus 4.6 due to ~60% refusals (App. C-C). Single run, no variance.

claims.claim: Gains come from programmatic harness enforcement, not prompting.
claims.evidence: Table IX four-tier ladder with Sonnet 4.6: T1 6 vulns/60% recall/33% FP; T2.5 11/60%/31%; T3 (Revelio harness) 14/80%/0%, $8.43/vuln. Small sample (recall values in 20-point steps imply ~10 cases), single run.

claims.claim: Results are not due to benchmark contamination.
claims.evidence: §V-B2: 10 post-cutoff CVEs with web search disabled show consistent ordering (App. B-B Table XII). Only 10 cases.

claims.claim: Cheap model for generation + strong model for confirmation is the most cost-effective configuration.
claims.evidence: Pilot sweep and ablation in App. C-A/C-B; Stage 2 is 57.84% of cost (App. D). Configuration chosen on the same pilot cases it is later compared on.

patterns.note: Sanitizer-confirmed PoV as deterministic verifier eliminates false positives (0% vs 28-60% for agents without enforced verification).
Per-stage model routing (Haiku for breadth, Sonnet for confirmation) matches or beats frontier single-model agents at similar cost per finding.
Hard stage break with structured artifact handoff between generation and confirmation outperforms prompt-described pipeline (Table IX).
General single-loop coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Sorcar) prompted with the same pipeline underperform the enforced harness.
Explicit caps (top-5 hypotheses, ≤5 PoV trials) and billed-cost accounting cross-checked against provider dashboards.
CyberGym used with modified file-localized protocol.

methodology.sample: 7 OSS-Fuzz projects (zero-day); 100 random memory-safety Arvo cases from CyberGym; 10 post-cutoff CVEs; 10-case pilot for config selection.
methodology.baselines: Claude Code v2.1.133 (Opus 4.7/4.6), Codex v0.125.0 (GPT 5.5), Sorcar v2026.05.35 (Opus 4.7), best model chosen per agent via pilot sweep; prompt-only tiers of Revelio itself.
methodology.models: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7, GPT 5.4 mini, GPT 5.4, GPT 5.5.
methodology.variance: Not reported; single runs per configuration.
methodology.ablations: Prompt vs harness ladder (Table IX); component ablation (App. C-B).
methodology.contamination_controls: Post-cutoff CVE set with web search disabled.

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/m1-llie/Revelio; prompts in Appendix A; benchmark manifest in Appendix B; raw results in Appendix C.

biases.detail: Authors define the FP metric via their own rerun+sanitizer check, which is Revelio's own acceptance criterion; baselines are not given the same enforced check.
Agentic runs are stochastic; no repeated runs or CIs.
Ablation ladder and fresh-CVE set are ~10 cases each; zero-day study is 7 projects.
Baselines run under a T2 natural-language prompt and Claude Code partially fell back to Opus 4.6 because of ~60% refusals, handicapping that baseline.
'AI agents are close to solving the problem of memory-safety vulnerability detection' extrapolated from a file-localized benchmark.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Anthropic and OpenAI models/agents used as baselines and backbones; Sorcar baseline is by co-author K. Sen (UC Berkeley).

verdict_reason: Externally validated zero-days (CVEs), an informative prompt-vs-harness ablation, released code and prompts, and a contamination check, though there are no repeated runs and the domain is C/C++ with sanitizer oracles only.
applicability: The harness lessons transfer even though the domain (C/C++ memory safety) does not. For the Java team: (1) enforce stage boundaries in code (spec → hypothesis → executable proof) instead of describing the pipeline in a prompt — the paper's T2.5→T3 jump shows prompt-described workflows leave high false-positive rates; (2) require a deterministic oracle before an agent claim is accepted (for repositories, a failing-then-passing JUnit/contract test plays the sanitizer's role); (3) route cheap models to broad scanning across the several repositories and reserve strong models for confirmation. Java lacks a sanitizer-equivalent for logic bugs, so the 0% FP result will not carry over directly.
